title: Judge who convicted cop in overdose death had 'hindsight bias,' appeal court told
article: An Indigenous woman who died of a drug overdose in police custody may still have still died had the arresting officer sought medical treatment for her, a lawyer for the London police officer told an appeal court.

A one-day hearing was held Wednesday for Const. Nicholas Doering, who was sentenced to one year in jail after he was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in the death of Debra Chrisjohn five years ago.

Doering, 31, arrested Chrisjohn, 39, in east London after she was found walking into traffic while high on crystal meth on Sept. 6, 2016. He transferred her into the custody of Elgin County OPP on an outstanding arrest warrant, falsely telling OPP officers that Chrisjohn had been medically assessed by paramedics.

Defence lawyer Alan Gold argued there was no evidence that Chrisjohn, a mother of 11, might have survived had medical treatment been provided, as stated in an agreed statement of facts from Doering's trial.
"There was no evidence that her chance of survival was anything other than minimal, minuscule," he said.
"If the death was likely, or very likely in any event with even the best medical assistance, then delay was not a significant contributing cause."

Soon after the OPP took Chrisjohn into custody, St. Thomas paramedics were called to the Elgin OPP detachment, where they found her motionless on the floor of her cell, breathing irregularly. Chrisjohn died later in hospital. A post-mortem found the cause of death was cardiac arrest connected to crystal meth use.

Gold further argued that Doering, who has experience dealing with meth users, and the OPP officers who took custody of Chrisjohn made a reasonable assumption that she was "riding out a high" and didn't need medical attention.
"Ms. Chrisjohn essentially took a poison. The problem was that the road to recovery and the road to fatality looked the same. There was no medical evidence disputing that proposition," Gold said.

Gold argued that the trial judge, Superior Court Justice Renee Pomerance, formed the opinion that Chrisjohn needed medical assistance and then interpreted the evidence through that lens, ignoring the opinions of multiple police officers experienced in dealing with intoxicated people.

"In my submission, the judge's approach really is an example of hindsight bias," Gold said. "The judge had never seen a methamphetamine overdose. These officers had. They reasonably formed a judgment. They were tragically wrong. Please don't misunderstand."
Crown counsel Jamie Klukach countered that Chrisjohn was "entirely dependent" on Doering for care and timely medical attention might have saved her life.
"That was her only shot at staying alive. She may have died, but Const. Doering denied her the opportunity to live," Klukach said.
Lawyers representing the Canadian Police Association, the Toronto Police Association and Police Association of Ontario also provided submissions Wednesday.

Doering, the first Canadian police officer convicted of criminal negligence causing death in an on-duty incident, has been suspended with pay since he was sentenced on Sept. 21, 2020. He was taken into custody briefly before being granted bail after his appeal was filed.
The appeals court will release its written decision at a later date.
